opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think robotics is exciting right now because a lot of the ingredients that made language models work are finally starting to line up for the physical world. For a long time, robotics was bottlenecked on very narrow, hand-engineered systems. You'd build a controller for one task in one environment, and it wouldn't generalize. Now we have these large pretrained models that carry a lot of common-sense knowledge about the world, and people are figuring out how to connect that knowledge to perception and action.

From my perspective, coming from the systems and efficiency side, robotics has some really interesting constraints. In language modeling you can often throw a big cluster at the problem and wait a few seconds for a response. With a robot, you need to run inference in real time, often on the device itself, with limited power and memory, and you're processing long streams of high-dimensional sensor data like video, proprioception, and audio. That's exactly the regime where efficient architectures matter a lot: long-context modeling, fast inference, state space models, hardware-aware kernels. The problems I've worked on map pretty naturally onto what robots need.

The other piece is data. Language models had the internet. Robotics doesn't have an equivalent, so there are open questions about how to collect data at scale, how to use simulation, how to transfer from video of humans, and how to make learning more sample-efficient. Those are hard, unsolved problems, and that's what makes it compelling as a research direction. It feels a bit like where language modeling was several years ago, where the right ideas could have an outsized impact.

And ultimately the payoff is huge. If AI can act in the physical world reliably, in homes, factories, healthcare, that's a massive change in what the technology can do for people. So it's both intellectually interesting and potentially very impactful, which is the combination I look for.

r001.rationale: The response mentions open research questions in robotics and says reliable AI in homes could have a major impact, but it does not identify capable humanoid robots working in homes as a source of those questions.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for me it comes down to where the interesting bottlenecks are. A lot of my work has been on making things like attention run efficiently on the hardware we have, and in language modeling we now have this pretty mature recipe: scale the data, scale the compute, make the kernels fast. Robotics is nowhere near that point, and that's exactly what makes it exciting.

The first thing is data. In language we have the internet, basically a free giant corpus. In robotics you don't get that. Every trajectory costs real time on a real robot, or you're simulating and then you have to deal with the sim-to-real gap. So the question of how you get enough signal to learn from is still wide open, and I think that pushes you toward ideas about pretraining on video, leveraging human demonstrations, and being much more careful about sample efficiency than we ever had to be for text.

The second thing is latency and the shape of the compute. A language model can take a few hundred milliseconds to think and nobody minds. A robot has a control loop, it has to act at tens or hundreds of hertz, and it's often running on hardware that's much more constrained than a datacenter GPU. So the systems questions I care about, memory bandwidth, how you structure the model so inference is cheap, how you handle long context over a stream of sensor inputs, all show up again but with different constraints. Things like state-space models or linear-time sequence layers become really attractive when you have a continuous stream and you can't afford to recompute over the whole history.

And then the third thing is just that it's a place where progress feels tangible. If you make the model better, the robot picks up the cup or it doesn't. There's something grounding about that compared to arguing over benchmark numbers. I don't think robotics is going to be solved by one clever architecture, but I do think a lot of the hard-won lessons from scaling language models, on both the modeling side and the systems side, haven't really been applied there yet, and that gap is where I want to spend time.

r001.rationale: The response identifies open robotics research questions around data and latency, but it does not present capable humanoid robots working in homes as their source.

astra-6.text:
I think robotics is exciting because it forces us to connect intelligence with action in the physical world. With language models, you can train on huge amounts of text and get feedback relatively cheaply. In robotics, collecting data is harder, and mistakes have physical consequences. You have to think about learning, perception, control, and the constraints of the hardware together.

From my perspective, that makes it a really interesting intersection of machine learning and systems. A model can’t just give a good answer eventually; it has to respond quickly enough to be useful. And there’s this fundamental question of generalization: can a robot take what it has learned and handle a new object or a new environment? Making progress on that would be exciting both scientifically and practically.

r001.rationale: The response raises open questions about robot learning and generalization, but does not mention capable humanoid robots working in homes as their source.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that robotics forces us to connect intelligence with action in the physical world. A model can produce a plausible answer, but a robot has to do something that actually works, with imperfect observations and limited time to react.

That brings together a lot of interesting problems: learning, planning, control, and efficient computation. You need models that are capable, but you also need them to run fast enough to be useful. And the feedback is very concrete: did the robot accomplish the task? I think that makes robotics a really exciting place to develop and test new ideas.

r001.rationale: The response describes robotics as an exciting area with challenges in learning, planning, and control, but it does not mention capable humanoid robots working in homes or present that prospect as a source of open research questions.
